name: Lesson 8 (RCP 202 + 203)
source: RCP 202 Lssn 8a/8b and RCP 203 Lssn 8a/8b lecture decks (slide text and speaker notes)

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: Who did the first lung transplant, when, and how long did the patient survive?
cards.a:
Who did the first lung transplant, when, and how long did the patient survive?
1963, Dr James Hardy. The patient survived 18 days; death resulted from renal failure.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What happened in 1983 and 1986 in lung transplantation?
cards.a:
What happened in 1983 and 1986 in lung transplantation?
1983: first successful lung transplant, a 58-year-old male with pulmonary fibrosis who survived 7 years.
1986: first double-lung transplant.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: Since when has lung transplantation been standard care for end-stage lung disease?
cards.a:
Since when has lung transplantation been standard care for end-stage lung disease?
Since 1983.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What are the four major disease groups for lung transplant?
cards.a:
What are the four major disease groups for lung transplant?
COPD/emphysema
Cystic fibrosis (CF)/bronchiectasis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: Which transplant indication is the most commonly debated?
cards.a:
Which transplant indication is the most commonly debated?
Pulmonary hypertension.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What trend has changed for IPF transplants, and why?
cards.a:
What trend has changed for IPF transplants, and why?
IPF used to be single lung, but over the past 15 years about 60% of IPF transplants are bilateral, because of better long-term survival plus better surgical techniques. Similar data exist for COPD patients under 60.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What are the referral criteria for IPF?
cards.a:
What are the referral criteria for IPF?
Resting hypoxemia, a decline in DLCO to <40% predicted, and development of group III pulmonary hypertension.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What are the common referral indications for CF?
cards.a:
What are the common referral indications for CF?
FEV1 <30% predicted, PaCO2 >50 mm Hg, PaO2 <55 mm Hg, massive hemoptysis, and recurrent pneumothoraces.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What are the referral criteria for COPD?
cards.a:
What are the referral criteria for COPD?
FEV1 <20% predicted, hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45 mm Hg), and homogeneous distribution that precludes lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What marks a good pulmonary hypertension candidate for transplant?
cards.a:
What marks a good pulmonary hypertension candidate for transplant?
NYHA functional class III or IV, uncompensated right heart failure, syncopal events, 6-minute walk <350 m, cardiac index <2 L/min/m², and right atrial pressure >15 mm Hg.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What is the 'transplant window'?
cards.a:
What is the 'transplant window'?
The ideal time is when tangible disease progression is observed but exertional capacity is not so limited that rehabilitation is no longer an option. It must balance disease progression against the patient's ability to rehabilitate.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Who decides transplant candidacy, and do all centers use the same criteria?
cards.a:
Who decides transplant candidacy, and do all centers use the same criteria?
Candidacy requires input from a multidisciplinary team plus several lab and radiographic investigations. Acceptable-recipient criteria vary among centers: a patient too high risk at one center may be average risk at another.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What are the GFR categories used in the transplant evaluation?
cards.a:
What are the GFR categories used in the transplant evaluation?
Normal: 90 mL/min/1.73 m² or above
Mild reduction: 60-89
Moderate reduction: 30-59
Severe reduction: 15-29
Kidney failure: less than 15

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What does a DEXA scan measure?
cards.a:
What does a DEXA scan measure?
Bone density and body composition (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What are HLAs and why are they compared in transplant recipients and donors?
cards.a:
What are HLAs and why are they compared in transplant recipients and donors?
Human leukocyte antigens are proteins on most body cells; the immune system uses them to tell native from foreign. A higher percentage of mismatch may preclude transplantation or require augmented immunosuppression.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Before May 2005, how were lung transplant patients selected, and what was the problem?
cards.a:
Before May 2005, how were lung transplant patients selected, and what was the problem?
By listing time. So patients with more slowly progressing diseases, such as COPD, were more likely to be transplanted.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What is the Lung Allocation Score (LAS)?
cards.a:
What is the Lung Allocation Score (LAS)?
Implemented May 2005, a scoring algorithm using clinical data to balance waitlist mortality and post-transplant survival. Applies to patients 12 and older, scored 0-100; higher score = shorter wait time.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What clinical factors go into the LAS (the deck's list)?
cards.a:
What clinical factors go into the LAS (the deck's list)?
Age, BMI, diagnosis, pulmonary function (e.g., FVC, oxygen requirement), functional status, heart and lung function (pulmonary artery pressure, cardiac output), and serum creatinine.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What replaced the geographic zones in lung allocation, and what are CAS and its effect?
cards.a:
What replaced the geographic zones in lung allocation, and what are CAS and its effect?
Continuous distribution replaced the binary geographic zones. Lungs are distributed by the composite allocation score (CAS), which still uses the LAS as a component and adds factors like proximity to the donor hospital. After it began in March 2023, transplant rates rose 16% and waiting-list mortality fell 29%.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: After continuous distribution began (March 2023), what were the transplant rates per 100 patient years?
cards.a:
After continuous distribution began (March 2023), what were the transplant rates per 100 patient years?
327 lung transplants per 100 patient years after the policy, compared with 281 before (a 16% increase).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What must the clinical exam show for brain death?
cards.a:
What must the clinical exam show for brain death?
Absent brain-originating motor response; absent corneal and oculovestibular reflexes; absent gag and cough despite tracheal suction; and a positive apnea test. Nuclear medicine or MRI may show absent cerebral blood flow.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: How is the apnea test done and what is a positive result?
cards.a:
How is the apnea test done and what is a positive result?
PaCO2 is normalized, then the patient is disconnected from the ventilator for up to 8 minutes (reconnected if respiratory activity occurs). Positive (consistent with brain death) = PaCO2 >60 mm Hg (or >20 mm Hg above baseline) and no breathing activity.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: When may DCDD be considered?
cards.a:
When may DCDD be considered?
In irreversible brain injury and end-stage musculoskeletal disease, where the patient does not meet criteria for brain death.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What is primary graft dysfunction (PGD)?
cards.a:
What is primary graft dysfunction (PGD)?
A type of acute lung injury within the first 72 hours after transplant; essentially reperfusion injury. A non-immune cause of early graft failure, similar to ARDS but in the transplanted lung.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What is bronchiolitis obliterans?
cards.a:
What is bronchiolitis obliterans?
An inflammatory obstruction of the tiniest airways (bronchioles), damaged by chemical particles or respiratory infections, particularly after organ transplants, leading to extensive scarring that blocks the airways.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What are the general donor-lung selection guidelines?
cards.a:
What are the general donor-lung selection guidelines?
Age <55 years; ABO compatible; PaO2 >300 on 1.0 O2 and +5 PEEP; no significant chest trauma or aspiration; no history of cardiopulmonary surgeries. Blood type and size (donor and recipient height) are essential; most centers keep their own criteria.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: How is the donor managed to preserve the lungs?
cards.a:
How is the donor managed to preserve the lungs?
Prevent interstitial fluid overload by monitoring PaO2 and keeping Pplat and PIP <30 cm H2O; diuretics and vasopressors to maintain MAP; optimize PEEP for oxygenation while watching venous return and cardiac output; desmopressin for diabetes insipidus after brain injury; consider thyroid hormone if hemodynamically unstable and/or EF <45%.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: Name ways to improve the suitability of donor lungs.
cards.a:
Name ways to improve the suitability of donor lungs.
Optimize donor management (hemodynamics, fluids, ventilation); ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP); infection and inflammation control; minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury (cooling, limiting cold ischemic time, preservation solutions like Perfadex); careful donor selection.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: At what temperature are donor lungs stored, and why?
cards.a:
At what temperature are donor lungs stored, and why?
4-8 °C, to decrease cellular metabolic activity and preserve cellular function.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Cold ischemic time versus ischemic time?
cards.a:
Cold ischemic time versus ischemic time?
Cold ischemic time: the organ is chilled without blood supply.
Ischemic time: time the organ remains at body or room temperature after blood supply is removed. Ischemia time should be minimized to prevent tissue injury and graft dysfunction.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: How does ischemic time relate to graft outcomes?
cards.a:
How does ischemic time relate to graft outcomes?
The acceptable limits of cold ischemic time are not known, but length of ischemic time directly correlates with risk of perfusion injury and primary graft dysfunction.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: What share of lung transplants today are single-lung?
cards.a:
What share of lung transplants today are single-lung?
Only 25%. In the pre-LAS era single-lung was the standard approach regardless of disease.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: How is infection handled early after lung transplant?
cards.a:
How is infection handled early after lung transplant?
Infection can be an early and prominent complication. Transplant ID specialists may use antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral agents. Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis and antiviral prophylaxis (targets CMV) are employed early.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What nutrition steps follow lung transplant?
cards.a:
What nutrition steps follow lung transplant?
Nutritional support is paramount. A swallowing study and FEES evaluate diet tolerance; patients may need a mechanically altered diet (dysphagia); more severe dysphagia may need gastrojejunal tubes (GJT).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: List the six postoperative management priorities after lung transplant (recap).
cards.a:
List the six postoperative management priorities after lung transplant (recap).
Lung-protective ventilation, management of primary graft dysfunction, chest tube removal, infection, nutritional support, and venous thromboembolism.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What is the primary FEV1 criterion for transplant in COPD (Stop and Think)?
cards.a:
What is the primary FEV1 criterion for transplant in COPD (Stop and Think)?
FEV1 typically less than 20-25% of predicted (slide 6 says <20%). FEV1 alone does not decide eligibility: evaluation also considers the BODE index (BMI, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, exercise capacity), exacerbation history and pulmonary hypertension. Also: frequent exacerbations or hospitalizations (especially acute hypercapnic respiratory failure), symptoms despite medications, oxygen and pulmonary rehab, and enough overall health to tolerate surgery and lifelong immunosuppression. Severe COPD alone does not automatically qualify a patient.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: How does the underlying disease affect single versus bilateral transplant?
cards.a:
How does the underlying disease affect single versus bilateral transplant?
The disease helps determine the procedure (the final decision also depends on the patient's condition, expected outcomes and donor availability). PAH generally requires bilateral transplant (replaces the diseased pulmonary vascular bed). IPF increasingly gets bilateral because of better long-term survival; single-lung is still an option. A similar advantage is seen in younger COPD patients. In PAH the right ventricle may recover after bilateral transplant because its afterload falls.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: Which transplant indication is the most commonly debated, and why?
cards.a:
Which transplant indication is the most commonly debated, and why?
Pulmonary hypertension. The concern is when transplant should occur, because newer PAH medications can delay the need for surgery.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::01 History, Disease States, Referral
cards.q: What is retransplantation and its most common cause?
cards.a:
What is retransplantation and its most common cause?
A second (or subsequent) lung transplant when the original lung(s) can no longer function adequately. The most common reason is chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD): progressive deterioration of the transplanted lungs, often associated with chronic rejection.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Does referral for transplant evaluation mean the patient is on the waiting list?
cards.a:
Does referral for transplant evaluation mean the patient is on the waiting list?
No. Referral for evaluation is not the same as listing. Early referral lets the team evaluate and prepare patients before they are too advanced. A patient does not have to be bedridden or ventilator-dependent to qualify; keeping mobility and muscle strength helps postoperative rehabilitation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Why does GERD matter in lung transplant patients?
cards.a:
Why does GERD matter in lung transplant patients?
Repeated microaspiration of gastric contents can injure the transplanted lungs and may contribute to chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Which conditions may preclude lung transplant (the corrected 'absolute contraindications' slide)?
cards.a:
Which conditions may preclude lung transplant (the corrected 'absolute contraindications' slide)?
The revised slide: high-risk malignancies, uncontrolled infections and active substance use may preclude transplant (the earlier slide called malignancy, chronic infection and substance abuse 'standard absolute contraindications'). The ideal recipient varies between centers. Some exclusion criteria are absolute, others relative (can be corrected or managed). Age alone is not an absolute contraindication: the table's age limit of over 60 is outdated and selected patients in their 60s and 70s are transplanted.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: What is emphasized about HLA matching in lung transplant?
cards.a:
What is emphasized about HLA matching in lung transplant?
Unlike kidney transplant, lung transplant does not routinely require a close HLA match. What matters is preexisting donor-specific HLA antibodies, which raise the risk of antibody-mediated rejection. (Rather than saying a high percentage of mismatch prevents transplant, emphasize these antibodies.)

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Why is the transplant patient typically relocated?
cards.a:
Why is the transplant patient typically relocated?
To be closer to the transplant and rehabilitation center. Patients may need to stay near the center before or after surgery depending on the center's requirements and distance; permanent relocation is not necessarily required. Patients and caregivers must also understand post-transplant expectations, including optimizing physical condition with pulmonary rehabilitation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: When did the Composite Allocation Score (CAS) replace the LAS, and what does it consider?
cards.a:
When did the Composite Allocation Score (CAS) replace the LAS, and what does it consider?
March 9, 2023. CAS uses a 0-100 score that considers medical urgency, expected post-transplant survival, biological matching challenges, patient access and organ placement efficiency. The LAS (0-100, introduced 2005) is no longer the current U.S. system.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::02 Recipient Selection & LAS
cards.q: Besides the LAS, what else is considered in lung allocation?
cards.a:
Besides the LAS, what else is considered in lung allocation?
Current allocation looks beyond medical urgency: blood type compatibility, chest cavity size, donor age, HLA profile and distance from the transplant center. Preservation time matters because donor lungs tolerate only a limited time without circulation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What are the two routes of lung donation, and which is more common?
cards.a:
What are the two routes of lung donation, and which is more common?
Donation after brain death (DBD) or after circulatory death (DCD). The majority of lung transplants use DBD. DCD is about 10% of cases, and the percentage varies by country and transplant program.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What must be true of the patient before brain death is determined?
cards.a:
What must be true of the patient before brain death is determined?
Stable with a normal core temperature (≥ 36 °C [96.8 °F]), SBP ≥ 100 mm Hg, MAP ≥ 75 mm Hg, eucapnia (normal PaCO2), absence of hypoxia, and euvolemia. (The slide prints '360 C [96.80 F]'; the superscripts were lost.) Hypothermia, hypotension, sedatives and metabolic disturbances must not be interfering with the exam.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What is brain death, and how is it diagnosed?
cards.a:
What is brain death, and how is it diagnosed?
Permanent loss of all brain function, including the brainstem (death by neurologic criteria). It is primarily a clinical diagnosis; ancillary testing is used only when indicated. A brain-dead patient may still have a heartbeat, warm skin and chest movement from the ventilator, which do not mean brain function remains.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What are the key facts about donation after circulatory determination of death (DCDD)?
cards.a:
What are the key facts about donation after circulatory determination of death (DCDD)?
Less common because ischemia time can make tissue nonviable. DCDD rose from 1 to 4% of U.S. lung transplants (2011 to 2016). Requires proof of absent circulation (A-line or Doppler) observed for 2 minutes. 60 to 120 minutes after withdrawal of life support is the upper limit for considering organ recovery, but acceptable limits depend on donor physiology, center protocols and preservation techniques. DCDD carries a greater risk of warm ischemia than brain-death donation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: How do DCDD lungs compare with brain-death lungs?
cards.a:
How do DCDD lungs compare with brain-death lungs?
The revised slide: DCD lungs may have greater warm ischemia, potentially raising the risk of early PGD and long-term BOS, but carefully selected DCD and DBD lungs can achieve comparable long-term outcomes. More recent studies suggest comparable survival without a consistently demonstrated increase in PGD or BOS. (The earlier slide said DCDD had a higher incidence of PGD and BOS with no survival difference.)

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::03 Donors
cards.q: What donor-management points did the revised notes add?
cards.a:
What donor-management points did the revised notes add?
Careful fluid management (excess IV fluid can contribute to pulmonary edema and may make lungs unsuitable); vasopressors for BP and diuretics for overload; PEEP helps recruitment but excess PEEP can reduce venous return and cardiac output. After brain death, damage to the hypothalamus and pituitary can cause central diabetes insipidus (low ADH): excessive urine, hypovolemia and hypernatremia. Desmopressin (DDAVP) replaces ADH activity.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Outline the donor lung procurement sequence.
cards.a:
Outline the donor lung procurement sequence.
Lungs are procured via median sternotomy; donor anticoagulated with IV heparin (prevents clotting in the pulmonary circulation); when blood pressure starts to fall the surgeon cross-clamps the aorta; lungs are filled with a chilled preservation solution, generally delivered through the pulmonary artery, flushing blood from the pulmonary vascular bed to prevent thrombosis and endothelial injury. Freezing must be avoided (ice crystals damage cell membranes and lung tissue).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Does cold preservation stop cellular metabolism?
cards.a:
Does cold preservation stop cellular metabolism?
No. Cooling to about 4-8 °C only slows metabolism and reduces oxygen demand, which is why minimizing preservation time still matters. Cold ischemic time: chilled without blood supply (cooling reduces, but does not eliminate, cellular metabolism).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: What is normothermic ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP)?
cards.a:
What is normothermic ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP)?
Donor lungs are ventilated and perfused outside the body with a warmed solution (lungs may first undergo initial cold preservation) to assess and optimize function and possibly rescue lungs first judged unsuitable. The deck cites 12 hours at body temperature but the revised slide says 12 hours is too restrictive: duration varies by system and protocol and some centers go longer.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Describe the single-lung transplant procedure.
cards.a:
Describe the single-lung transplant procedure.
Posterolateral or anterolateral thoracotomy; one-lung ventilation (the non-operative lung is ventilated, the operative lung collapsed); pulmonary artery of the diseased lung clamped; extracorporeal support may be indicated but is not required for every single-lung transplant. Anastomoses order: bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins to a left atrial cuff. Air is purged and three chest tubes are placed (anterior, posterior, basilar).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Why can one-lung ventilation cause hypoxemia during the transplant?
cards.a:
Why can one-lung ventilation cause hypoxemia during the transplant?
The nonventilated lung still receives some pulmonary blood flow, creating an intrapulmonary shunt, so oxygenation must be monitored closely throughout.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Describe the bilateral lung transplant procedure.
cards.a:
Describe the bilateral lung transplant procedure.
Transverse thoracosternotomy (clamshell; other approaches are possible) with lungs implanted sequentially. The worst-functioning native lung is removed first while the other lung is ventilated; single-lung ventilation then moves to the allograft. The new first lung must support ventilation during the second implant and is vulnerable to reperfusion injury. Chest tubes are placed bilaterally; their number varies by surgeon and institution.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: Compare CPB and ECMO cannulation for lung transplant.
cards.a:
Compare CPB and ECMO cannulation for lung transplant.
CPB: right atrium and ascending aorta (a common central approach; other configurations are possible).
ECMO: typically femoral or jugular access. V-V drains vena cava/right atrium and returns to the right atrium; V-A drains the right atrium and returns to the arterial system. ECMO may have fewer complications than CPB. Both are used as a bridge and intraoperatively.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::04 Procurement & Surgery
cards.q: What is the difference between V-V and V-A ECMO in lung transplant?
cards.a:
What is the difference between V-V and V-A ECMO in lung transplant?
V-V: respiratory support only (oxygenation and CO2 removal), returns blood to the venous circulation, does not directly support the heart.
V-A: respiratory plus circulatory support, returns blood to the arterial circulation. V-A is often preferred in transplant when support is needed, especially with severe pulmonary hypertension or right ventricular dysfunction, because it supports circulation during PA clamping and implantation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What are the general postoperative ventilator guidelines after lung transplant?
cards.a:
What are the general postoperative ventilator guidelines after lung transplant?
Lung-protective: VT about 6 mL/kg PBW (≤6), PEEP starting around 5 cm H2O, FiO2 ≤0.5 titrated to adequate oxygenation, plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O. Consider ECMO for severe refractory respiratory or circulatory failure. The revised notes say PEEP ≤5 is too restrictive as a universal rule (individualize; higher may be needed) and 0.5 is a goal, not an absolute limit. The earlier slide said 'PEEP no higher than 5'.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: Why can ventilating a single-lung transplant in a COPD patient cause overdistension?
cards.a:
Why can ventilating a single-lung transplant in a COPD patient cause overdistension?
The native and transplanted lungs have different compliance. In COPD the remaining native lung may be more compliant and receive a greater share of the VT, raising the risk of overdistension.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What is the greatest postoperative challenge, and how is it graded?
cards.a:
What is the greatest postoperative challenge, and how is it graded?
Primary graft dysfunction (PGD), within the first 72 hours, mainly from ischemia-reperfusion injury (more capillary permeability, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, impaired oxygenation, ARDS-like). Graded 0 to 3 by P/F ratio and chest imaging infiltrates; severe PGD may also decrease compliance and increase pulmonary vascular resistance. Treatment is supportive: lung-protective ventilation, careful fluids, ECMO in severe cases.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: When and in what order are chest tubes removed after lung transplant?
cards.a:
When and in what order are chest tubes removed after lung transplant?
Sequentially over about 7-10 days: mediastinal, anterior, posterior, then basilar, after several days of output ≤100-150 mL. The revised slide says removal depends on drainage, air leaks and lung expansion, not a fixed schedule, and the 100-150 mL threshold is institution-dependent.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What infection prevention follows lung transplant?
cards.a:
What infection prevention follows lung transplant?
Lifelong immunosuppression raises the risk of bacterial, fungal and viral infection. Preventive drugs are common, especially against Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJP) and cytomegalovirus (CMV), chosen by infection risk, donor and recipient screening, and center protocol.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: Why is the FEES swallowing study useful after lung transplant?
cards.a:
Why is the FEES swallowing study useful after lung transplant?
FEES (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing) is particularly useful for identifying aspiration, including silent aspiration (no obvious coughing or choking). Even small amounts of aspirated food or gastric contents can injure the transplanted lungs.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: How is VTE managed after lung transplant?
cards.a:
How is VTE managed after lung transplant?
Low-dose subcutaneous heparin as early as postop day one, when bleeding risk permits per center protocol. Early ambulation, PT and OT reduce venous stasis (preventing DVT) and improve lung expansion (reducing atelectasis). Mobilization can start once stable, even on a ventilator.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What is the cornerstone of ventilator management after lung transplant?
cards.a:
What is the cornerstone of ventilator management after lung transplant?
Lung-protective ventilation using appropriate PEEP and the lowest FiO2 necessary to maintain adequate oxygenation. (The earlier slide said 'minimization of PEEP and FiO2'.)

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8a Lung Transplant::05 Postoperative Management
cards.q: What reduces postoperative complications in lung transplant, and what extracorporeal support may be needed?
cards.a:
What reduces postoperative complications in lung transplant, and what extracorporeal support may be needed?
Minimizing warm and cold ischemic times. Recipients may need intraoperative or postoperative extracorporeal support (CPB or ECMO): CPB is primarily used intraoperatively, ECMO may be used before, during or after transplant.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What does the NBRC exam cover for Section III-D (Administer Medications and Specialty Gases)?
cards.a:
What does the NBRC exam cover for Section III-D (Administer Medications and Specialty Gases)?
TMC: 4 questions (used to be 5): 1 recall (used to be 2) and 3 application. CSE: an indeterminate number, but III-D knowledge is a prerequisite, especially for Information Gathering.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: When are aerosolized antibiotics (colistin, Cayston, TOBI) generally indicated?
cards.a:
When are aerosolized antibiotics (colistin, Cayston, TOBI) generally indicated?
Generally only in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) and suspected or confirmed Pseudomonas aeruginosa (gram-negative) pulmonary infection.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: In what order should several inhaled medications be given?
cards.a:
In what order should several inhaled medications be given?
Bronchodilator first, then mucolytic, then airway clearance therapy, then steroids, finally the aerosolized antibiotic.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: Which beta agonist should you recommend, and why?
cards.a:
Which beta agonist should you recommend, and why?
Those with the least β1 (cardiac) and most β2 (bronchodilation) effects, i.e., albuterol or its isomer levalbuterol. All beta agonists have some cardiovascular and CNS effects.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: Which drugs are 'relievers' and which are 'controllers'?
cards.a:
Which drugs are 'relievers' and which are 'controllers'?
Short-acting beta agonists (SABAs) are best used as relievers of bronchospasm; long-acting beta agonists (LABAs) and/or steroids are best used as controllers.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: How do you dose a bronchodilator in an acute asthma exacerbation?
cards.a:
How do you dose a bronchodilator in an acute asthma exacerbation?
Repeat the standard dose every 20 minutes (up to 3 times) or give continuous nebulization until symptoms are relieved.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What are the LABA cautions in asthma?
cards.a:
What are the LABA cautions in asthma?
LABAs may increase the risk of severe exacerbations/death in some asthmatics (they mask airway inflammation). They should generally be used with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and should not be recommended or used to treat acute exacerbations.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What can be used for maintenance therapy of bronchospasm in COPD?
cards.a:
What can be used for maintenance therapy of bronchospasm in COPD?
A LABA (salmeterol), a long-acting anticholinergic (tiotropium), or a LABA plus long-acting anticholinergic combination (umeclidinium + vilanterol).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: Which LABA is available as a nebulizer solution?
cards.a:
Which LABA is available as a nebulizer solution?
Arformoterol, the (R,R) enantiomer of formoterol, is the only LABA available as an inhalation solution for a nebulizer.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What is the cromolyn sodium note?
cards.a:
What is the cromolyn sodium note?
Prevents onset and development of the asthmatic response by inhibiting chemical mediators of inflammation. Given via SVN; the CFC version was removed from the market as of 12/31/2010.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What must you remember when giving mucokinetics?
cards.a:
What must you remember when giving mucokinetics?
All mucokinetics are irritating to the airway, so always PRECEDE treatment with a bronchodilator to prevent bronchospasm, and give them with airway clearance therapy to remove secretions.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What do inhaled corticosteroids do, and what are the key delivery points?
cards.a:
What do inhaled corticosteroids do, and what are the key delivery points?
They control inflammation and are first-line for mild persistent asthma. Except budesonide (Pulmicort), common inhaled steroids are for MDI or DPI only, so technique is critical. Rinse the mouth afterward to prevent pharyngitis and oral candidiasis; spacers (valved holding chambers) with MDI steroids minimize pharyngeal deposition.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: Which inhaled corticosteroids does the deck list, and which LABA/ICS combinations exist?
cards.a:
Which inhaled corticosteroids does the deck list, and which LABA/ICS combinations exist?
ICS: fluticasone (Flovent), budesonide (Pulmicort Flexhaler), mometasone (Asmanex), flunisolide, beclomethasone (Qvar), ciclesonide (Alvesco).
Combinations: fluticasone + salmeterol (Advair Diskus), budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort), mometasone + formoterol (Dulera), fluticasone + vilanterol (Breo Ellipta).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::01 Aerosolized Drug Considerations
cards.q: What is oral thrush (oral candidiasis)?
cards.a:
What is oral thrush (oral candidiasis)?
The fungus Candida albicans accumulating on the lining of the mouth, causing creamy white lesions usually on the tongue or inner cheeks. More likely in babies, older adults, immunosuppressed people, and those on chronic systemic steroids or antibiotics.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: How do you choose an aerosol delivery device?
cards.a:
How do you choose an aerosol delivery device?
First determine the available formulations (some drugs come in only one form). If several exist, assess the patient. In many cases the drug formulation dictates the choice; otherwise acuity, age, inspiratory flows, and ability to use an MDI decide. If several devices qualify, patient preference decides.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: When should a small volume nebulizer (SVN) be used?
cards.a:
When should a small volume nebulizer (SVN) be used?
SVN administration should be reserved for acutely ill adults who cannot use a DPI or MDI.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: What is the preferred device for most infants and small children?
cards.a:
What is the preferred device for most infants and small children?
An MDI with a holding chamber and mask (SVN is an alternative if tolerated).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: What if an adult who is not acutely ill can't coordinate MDI actuation with breathing?
cards.a:
What if an adult who is not acutely ill can't coordinate MDI actuation with breathing?
Consider adding a holding chamber; a breath-actuated MDI is an alternative.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: What should patients prescribed steroids by MDI use?
cards.a:
What should patients prescribed steroids by MDI use?
Either a spacer or a holding chamber, to minimize pharyngeal deposition.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: When are DPIs ideal?
cards.a:
When are DPIs ideal?
For maintenance therapy in outpatient adults, larger children, and adolescents who can generate sufficient inspiratory flow to carry the powder into the lungs.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: Where do you place the adapter for aerosol delivery with CPAP/BiPAP?
cards.a:
Where do you place the adapter for aerosol delivery with CPAP/BiPAP?
The T-adaptor for SVN or MDI adaptor near the mask or other patient interface.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: Which gas should drive an SVN used with BiPAP?
cards.a:
Which gas should drive an SVN used with BiPAP?
The gas source (air vs. O2) and flow should approximate the FiO2 delivered to the patient. If the patient is on a high FiO2, use oxygen to drive the nebulizer.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::02 Aerosol Delivery Systems
cards.q: What precautions apply to neonates and infants when nebulizing on CPAP/BiPAP?
cards.a:
What precautions apply to neonates and infants when nebulizing on CPAP/BiPAP?
Use a blender for a precise FiO2 for the gas driving the nebulizer and continuously monitor pulse oximetry to minimize oxygen risks.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: Which drugs can be given by endotracheal instillation in emergencies, and what is the mnemonic?
cards.a:
Which drugs can be given by endotracheal instillation in emergencies, and what is the mnemonic?
Lidocaine, Epinephrine, Atropine, Naloxone (L-E-A-N) when IV access is not available; some add vasopressin (N-A-V-E-L).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: What are the guidelines for endotracheal instillation of LEAN drugs?
cards.a:
What are the guidelines for endotracheal instillation of LEAN drugs?
Dose 2-2.5 times the IV dose; dilute with 10 mL of sterile water or saline; patient supine (not Trendelenburg); halt chest compressions; instill through a catheter that passes beyond the ETT tip; then give 5-10 rapid inflations with a bag-valve-mask.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: Trendelenburg versus reverse Trendelenburg?
cards.a:
Trendelenburg versus reverse Trendelenburg?
Trendelenburg: head down, feet up. Reverse Trendelenburg: head up, feet down.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: When is surfactant given?
cards.a:
When is surfactant given?
Prophylactically to infants at high risk of developing RDS, or as rescue therapy for infants with clinical evidence of RDS.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: What are the steps before and during surfactant instillation?
cards.a:
What are the steps before and during surfactant instillation?
Recommend a CXR before instillation to confirm ETT position; suction first if necessary; monitor SpO2 and ECG continuously; use a 5-Fr feeding tube or suction catheter; insert it up to, but not past, the ETT tip; split the dose in half into each dependent bronchus (turning the infant side to side); give it as rapidly as tolerated.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: What happens after surfactant administration?
cards.a:
What happens after surfactant administration?
Manually ventilate 1-2 minutes; monitor ABGs and chest movement during the first 3 hours; adjust ventilator settings and FiO2 (the patient may transiently need more support); if possible, avoid suctioning for 6 hours.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::03 Instillation
cards.q: What does surfactant do?
cards.a:
What does surfactant do?
Reduces surface tension (prevents alveolar collapse on exhalation), stabilizes alveoli, facilitates gas exchange, and has immune-modulating properties that help protect against infection.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: Why is helium useful in respiratory care?
cards.a:
Why is helium useful in respiratory care?
Its low density. A heliox mixture (80/20% or 70/30%) decreases the driving pressure needed in ventilation, particularly in large airways, so it can decrease the WOB of large airway obstruction.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: What are the major indications for heliox?
cards.a:
What are the major indications for heliox?
Acute upper airway obstruction, reversible obstructive disorders, post-extubation stridor, and croup.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: How is heliox usually delivered, and what premixed cylinders exist?
cards.a:
How is heliox usually delivered, and what premixed cylinders exist?
Via premixed cylinders through a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask, with flow meeting or exceeding the patient's minute ventilation and peak inspiratory flow, or via high-flow nasal cannula. Cylinders: 80%, 70%, or 60% He in 20%, 30% or 40% O2.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: Why is heliox by oxyhood limited in infants with bronchiolitis?
cards.a:
Why is heliox by oxyhood limited in infants with bronchiolitis?
Heat loss and hypothermia from helium's high thermal conductivity; high-flow nasal cannula is now preferred in this population.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: How do you adjust flow when heliox powers a nebulizer?
cards.a:
How do you adjust flow when heliox powers a nebulizer?
Increase flows by 50-100%. Heliox's low density reduces nebulizer efficiency at lower flow rates, decreasing the inhaled medication dose.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: What monitoring is required for patients receiving heliox?
cards.a:
What monitoring is required for patients receiving heliox?
Close monitoring and an O2 analyzer with active alarms to measure the FiO2 delivered.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: Why combine heliox with jet-nebulized bronchodilators?
cards.a:
Why combine heliox with jet-nebulized bronchodilators?
To treat severe acute obstructive disorders such as status asthmaticus, especially when standard therapy fails; it may improve delivery and deposition of aerosolized drugs.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::04 Heliox
cards.q: What is acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus), and when should steroids be given?
cards.a:
What is acute severe asthma (status asthmaticus), and when should steroids be given?
Severe asthma unresponsive to repeated courses of beta-agonist therapy (albuterol, levalbuterol, or subcutaneous epinephrine); a medical emergency. Give oral or parenteral corticosteroids as early as possible, because benefit may take a minimum of 6-12 hours.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What does inhaled nitric oxide (NO) do?
cards.a:
What does inhaled nitric oxide (NO) do?
A potent pulmonary vasodilator that relaxes the smooth muscle of pulmonary vessels. It can reduce intrapulmonary shunting, improve arterial oxygenation, and decrease pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressures.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What is inhaled NO approved for?
cards.a:
What is inhaled NO approved for?
Term and near-term (>34 weeks' gestation) neonates with hypoxemic respiratory failure associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: Has inhaled NO improved long-term outcomes in adults with ARDS-related pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a:
Has inhaled NO improved long-term outcomes in adults with ARDS-related pulmonary hypertension?
It has been used for pulmonary hypertension associated with ARDS, but no significant improvement in long-term clinical outcomes has been shown.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: How is inhaled NO delivered?
cards.a:
How is inhaled NO delivered?
More commonly to mechanically ventilated patients (can be given by NC or mask). Systems (INOvent, INOmax) use storage cylinders and an injector in the inspiratory limb near the ventilator outlet with a flow sensor; the injection rate is automatically adjusted in proportion to measured gas flow.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What is the recommended initial dose of inhaled NO?
cards.a:
What is the recommended initial dose of inhaled NO?
20 ppm, which can often be quickly reduced to 5-6 ppm. Treatment may continue for up to 14 days.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What toxic by-product forms when NO contacts oxygen?
cards.a:
What toxic by-product forms when NO contacts oxygen?
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2). INO equipment limits the contact time between the gases to minimize NO2 production.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What are the factors to consider before withdrawing inhaled NO?
cards.a:
What are the factors to consider before withdrawing inhaled NO?
Reduce NO to the lowest effective dose, ideally 5-6 ppm or less; ensure the patient is hemodynamically stable; verify tolerance of FiO2 40% or less and PEEP 5 cm H2O or less; monitor closely during withdrawal; be prepared to provide hemodynamic support.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: Which aerosolized medications (not gases) treat pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a:
Which aerosolized medications (not gases) treat pulmonary hypertension?
Iloprost (Ventavis), treprostinil (Tyvasco), epoprostenol (Flolan). They dilate pulmonary arterial beds and decrease platelet aggregation, reducing intrapulmonary shunting and improving oxygenation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 203 · 8a Ch 12 Meds & Gases::05 Nitric Oxide and Inhaled Vasodilators
cards.q: What are the five groups of pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a:
What are the five groups of pulmonary hypertension?
Group 1: pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)
Group 2: due to left-sided heart disease
Group 3: due to lung disease and/or hypoxia
Group 4: due to pulmonary artery obstructions, including CTEPH
Group 5: unknown and/or multiple causes

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What are postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) and how common are they?
cards.a:
What are postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) and how common are they?
Unexpected postoperative pulmonary abnormalities that produce identifiable disease or dysfunction, are clinically important and need therapeutic intervention. They occur in about 7% of patients with normal preoperative lung function and have been reported as high as 70% in patients with increased risk factors.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What does obesity do to surgical risk?
cards.a:
What does obesity do to surgical risk?
Surgical mortality is not increased in obese patients, but morbidly obese patients are at increased risk of reduced lung volumes (atelectasis), V/Q mismatch, and persistent hypoxemia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What is the STOP-BANG questionnaire used for?
cards.a:
What is the STOP-BANG questionnaire used for?
A validated screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in the preoperative setting.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What do the letters in STOP-BANG stand for?
cards.a:
What do the letters in STOP-BANG stand for?
Snoring (loud), Tired (daytime), Observed (stops breathing in sleep), Pressure (high blood pressure), BMI >35, Age >50, Neck size large (>16 inches / 40 cm), Gender = male.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: Which factors are risk factors for postoperative respiratory complications (Key Points)?
cards.a:
Which factors are risk factors for postoperative respiratory complications (Key Points)?
Age, smoking history, preexisting lung disease, and poor nutritional status.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What advice would you give a 68-year-old, 280-lb current smoker before surgery (Stop and Think)?
cards.a:
What advice would you give a 68-year-old, 280-lb current smoker before surgery (Stop and Think)?
Smoking cessation as soon as possible (even short-term helps); weight loss/management if time permits; optimize comorbid conditions. For the care team: thorough preoperative evaluation (cardiac and pulmonary), preoperative PFTs, postoperative respiratory support (incentive spirometry or chest physiotherapy), VTE prophylaxis, and closer postoperative monitoring.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraoperative and Postoperative Management
cards.q: Which complications occur frequently after surgery?
cards.a:
Which complications occur frequently after surgery?
Atelectasis, infection, respiratory failure, exacerbations of underlying chronic lung disease, and bronchospasm.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: How much basal lung collapses after induction of general anesthesia, and what FiO2 contributes?
cards.a:
How much basal lung collapses after induction of general anesthesia, and what FiO2 contributes?
20% to 25% of basal lung tissue collapses after induction. High oxygen concentrations (more than 40%) contribute to collapse.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What are the signs and symptoms of atelectasis?
cards.a:
What are the signs and symptoms of atelectasis?
Inspiratory crackles, bronchial breath sounds, diminished breath sounds, increased RR and dyspnea, increased HR, and hypoxemia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: What are the signs and symptoms of acute PE?
cards.a:
What are the signs and symptoms of acute PE?
Abrupt onset of cough, pleuritic chest pain, anxiety, tachycardia, hypoxemia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: How is PE prophylaxis done in hospitalized patients?
cards.a:
How is PE prophylaxis done in hospitalized patients?
Prevent DVT: intermittent pneumatic compression devices, plus early ambulation and leg exercises.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: When is heparin anticoagulation therapeutic, and what can't anticoagulants do?
cards.a:
When is heparin anticoagulation therapeutic, and what can't anticoagulants do?
When the clotting time or PTT is 2 to 2.5 times the control. Anticoagulants prevent further clot formation but will not dissolve clots already present.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: What dissolves existing clots, and what is the caution?
cards.a:
What dissolves existing clots, and what is the caution?
Thrombolytic therapy, commonly tissue plasminogen activator (TPA). Balance its usefulness against the risk of bleeding in postoperative patients.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: What is a 'bird's nest' filter?
cards.a:
What is a 'bird's nest' filter?
An inferior vena cava (IVC) filter placed to prevent clots that originate in the lower extremities from reaching the lungs.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: What drugs besides heparin can be used for patients at increased risk of thromboembolism?
cards.a:
What drugs besides heparin can be used for patients at increased risk of thromboembolism?
Warfarin and newer anticoagulants (e.g., Eliquis).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: How common is postoperative pneumonia?
cards.a:
How common is postoperative pneumonia?
The third most common complication in postoperative patients; reported in 18% of patients undergoing elective upper or lower abdominal and thoracic surgery. Nosocomial pneumonia (more than 48 hours after admission) is 15% of all hospital-acquired infections, with half occurring in surgical patients.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: What are the risk factors for postoperative pneumonia?
cards.a:
What are the risk factors for postoperative pneumonia?
Immunosuppression, malnutrition, COPD, and age >65.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 PE and Pneumonia
cards.q: Mucous versus purulent sputum?
cards.a:
Mucous versus purulent sputum?
Mucous: clear or translucent and viscous, with only small numbers of microscopic elements.
Purulent: off-white, yellow or green, and opaque; indicates large numbers of white blood cells, especially neutrophils.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: What is the goal of preoperative evaluation, and what is the important first step?
cards.a:
What is the goal of preoperative evaluation, and what is the important first step?
Goal: identify patients at risk for intraoperative or postoperative complications. First step: obtain a patient history and physical exam. Preoperative patient education is important.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: When is a preoperative ECG important?
cards.a:
When is a preoperative ECG important?
For the patient with a history of circulatory and cardiac problems.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: When are preoperative ABGs indicated?
cards.a:
When are preoperative ABGs indicated?
In patients with new or changing lung disease and in those at high risk for lung disease.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: Who should have preoperative PFTs?
cards.a:
Who should have preoperative PFTs?
PFTs are recommended for all patients who are candidates for lung resection.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk and Preoperative Assessment
cards.q: Does routine preoperative screening of healthy patients change outcomes?
cards.a:
Does routine preoperative screening of healthy patients change outcomes?
Little evidence exists that routine screening of healthy patients with ECGs, CXRs, PFTs, echocardiograms, or blood chemistry panels significantly alters outcomes.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraoperative and Postoperative Management
cards.q: What intraoperative factors affect postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a:
What intraoperative factors affect postoperative pulmonary complications?
Surgical incision site, duration of surgery, type of anesthesia, monitoring during anesthesia, intraoperative fluid management, and ventilator settings (VT and PEEP).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraoperative and Postoperative Management
cards.q: What VT and PEEP should be used during surgery (lung-protective ventilation)?
cards.a:
What VT and PEEP should be used during surgery (lung-protective ventilation)?
6-8 mL/kg of predicted (ideal) body weight and low levels of PEEP. Also limit Pplat to less than 30 cm H2O and use the lowest FiO2 needed.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraoperative and Postoperative Management
cards.q: What does lung-protective ventilation in the OR aim to minimize, and what does it reduce?
cards.a:
What does lung-protective ventilation in the OR aim to minimize, and what does it reduce?
It minimizes volutrauma (low VT) and atelectrauma (PEEP). It is associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications (respiratory failure and pneumonia).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraoperative and Postoperative Management
cards.q: List the components of postoperative respiratory management.
cards.a:
List the components of postoperative respiratory management.
Pain control, mobilization, lung expansion therapy, airway clearance, ventilator liberation, nutritional support, oxygen therapy.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: Does atelectasis cause fever?
cards.a:
Does atelectasis cause fever?
Atelectasis without infection does not result in fever (contrary to common teaching). Fever with atelectasis is most often infection from retained secretions.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: Where are bronchial breath sounds normal, and what does hearing them over the lung periphery mean?
cards.a:
Where are bronchial breath sounds normal, and what does hearing them over the lung periphery mean?
Normally heard over the trachea or manubrium (loud, high-pitched, harsh, tubular, with a longer expiratory phase and a pause between phases). Over peripheral lung they suggest consolidation: air-filled alveoli replaced by solid tissue or fluid (e.g., lobar pneumonia, atelectasis with a patent bronchus).

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: How does the revised deck characterize pulmonary complications as a cause of postoperative morbidity and death?
cards.a:
How does the revised deck characterize pulmonary complications as a cause of postoperative morbidity and death?
The revised slide calls pulmonary complications a major cause of postoperative morbidity and death; the earlier slide said the leading cause. Notes retain that PPCs occur more frequently than postoperative cardiac complications and prolong ICU and hospital stays.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: How does age affect postoperative risk?
cards.a:
How does age affect postoperative risk?
About 1/3 of inpatient surgeries involve patients older than 65. The revised slide emphasizes increasing risk with comorbidities or frailty and altered inflammatory responses; the earlier slide gave a fixed complication estimate and described an increased inflammatory response.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Why does pulmonary function fall after thoracic or upper abdominal surgery?
cards.a:
Why does pulmonary function fall after thoracic or upper abdominal surgery?
The revised slide describes increased risk, whereas the earlier slide said most patients would decline. Reduced lung volumes, diaphragmatic dysfunction, and V/Q mismatch impair gas exchange. Notes add that anesthesia may depress the postoperative respiratory drive and that inhibited cough and impaired airway clearance add infection risk.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: When are preoperative chest radiographs indicated?
cards.a:
When are preoperative chest radiographs indicated?
The revised slide says to consider CXR for new or worsening cardiopulmonary symptoms or when findings may influence perioperative management. The earlier slide used broader disease and risk categories. Testing should follow the patient's history, symptoms, and planned procedure.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraop
cards.q: What pulmonary complication rate do upper abdominal and thoracic surgeries carry?
cards.a:
What pulmonary complication rate do upper abdominal and thoracic surgeries carry?
The revised slide retains an approximate pulmonary complication rate of 20% to 70% for thoracic and upper abdominal surgery. It emphasizes increased risk because surgical pain and diaphragmatic dysfunction can limit lung expansion and promote atelectasis.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraop
cards.q: Why does intraoperative fluid management matter?
cards.a:
Why does intraoperative fluid management matter?
The revised slide emphasizes both excessive and inadequate fluid administration; the earlier slide focused on adequate replacement and organ function. Excess fluid may contribute to pulmonary edema, while inadequate replacement can reduce organ perfusion and oxygen delivery.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What does the evidence say about IPPB and incentive spirometry?
cards.a:
What does the evidence say about IPPB and incentive spirometry?
The revised slide says evidence does not support routine incentive spirometry alone to prevent PPCs; the earlier slide grouped IPPB and incentive spirometry in a broader negative statement. Notes place IS within a recovery strategy including deep breathing, mobilization, and pain control.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: List the postoperative respiratory management measures in the Key Points.
cards.a:
List the postoperative respiratory management measures in the Key Points.
The revised slide lists pain control, early mobilization, deep breathing, indicated lung expansion and airway clearance therapies, ventilator liberation, nutritional support, and oxygen as needed. The earlier slide said early feeding and early ventilator liberation; the revision makes therapy selection conditional.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What is atelectasis and how common is it after surgery?
cards.a:
What is atelectasis and how common is it after surgery?
Atelectasis is reversible collapse of previously expanded alveoli, reducing lung volume and impairing gas exchange. It is reported in 90% of anesthetized patients. The slide calls it the most common noninfectious complication; notes say one of the most common.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What are the radiographic signs of atelectasis?
cards.a:
What are the radiographic signs of atelectasis?
Look for increased opacity with volume loss, displaced fissures, elevated diaphragm, and mediastinal shift toward the affected side. The revised slide clarifies that air bronchograms may occur but can be absent with complete airway obstruction; the earlier list presented them without that qualification.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: How is postoperative atelectasis prevented and managed?
cards.a:
How is postoperative atelectasis prevented and managed?
Use education, coughing, deep breathing, mobilization, pain control, and indicated lung expansion or airway clearance therapies. Oxygen treats hypoxemia; severe respiratory failure may require ventilation. The revised slide adds pain control and clarifies that smoking cessation chiefly supports preoperative preparation and long-term pulmonary health.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What are the benefits of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)?
cards.a:
What are the benefits of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)?
PCA offers patient involvement, potentially less drug use, faster analgesia, and better pain control. The revised slide omits the earlier minimal-side-effects wording, although retained notes still use it. New notes stress programmed dosing, lockout intervals, and monitoring for opioid-related respiratory depression.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 Thromboembolism & PE
cards.q: What is the most common cause of PE, and how do DVTs form in surgical patients?
cards.a:
What is the most common cause of PE, and how do DVTs form in surgical patients?
The most common cause is VTE, usually clots from leg veins traveling to pulmonary vessels. The revised slide expands the earlier venostasis explanation to Virchow's triad: venous stasis, vascular injury, and increased coagulability, particularly after surgery or prolonged immobility.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 Thromboembolism & PE
cards.q: How is PE diagnosed?
cards.a:
How is PE diagnosed?
The revised slide specifies CT pulmonary angiography with IV contrast, replacing the earlier generic CT angiography wording. CTPA is commonly preferred when appropriate. A V/Q scan is an alternative when CTPA is unsuitable, showing perfusion defects with relatively preserved ventilation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::04 Thromboembolism & PE
cards.q: List the management options for PE.
cards.a:
List the management options for PE.
Options include DVT prevention, anticoagulation, selected thrombolysis, IVC filters, and catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy. The revised slide expands the earlier surgery-only wording. Notes make anticoagulation primary for most patients and reserve filters and clot-removal interventions for selected situations.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::05 Pneumonia & Ventilation
cards.q: What are the signs and symptoms of postoperative pneumonia?
cards.a:
What are the signs and symptoms of postoperative pneumonia?
The revised slide lists fever, chills, productive cough with purulent sputum, hemoptysis, tachypnea, dyspnea, crackles or bronchial breath sounds, hypoxemia, and pleuritic pain. It replaces the earlier dullness-to-percussion wording with bronchial breath sounds and explicitly adds dyspnea and hypoxemia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::05 Pneumonia & Ventilation
cards.q: How is postoperative pneumonia managed?
cards.a:
How is postoperative pneumonia managed?
The revised slide specifies antibiotics guided by suspected pathogens and cultures, oxygen, airway clearance for retained secretions, and ventilation with appropriate PEEP for severe respiratory failure. The earlier slide listed antibiotics, oxygen, and ventilation without these treatment-selection qualifications.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::05 Pneumonia & Ventilation
cards.q: Why might a patient need mechanical ventilation after surgery, and what is the risk?
cards.a:
Why might a patient need mechanical ventilation after surgery, and what is the risk?
The revised slide broadens the earlier residual-anesthesia explanation to inadequate ventilation or oxygenation and surgical complications. Prolonged invasive ventilation increases VAP risk. Use lung-protective ventilation, preventive measures, timely extubation, and NIV for selected patients.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: What are PPCs, and how does baseline risk affect their frequency?
cards.a:
What are PPCs, and how does baseline risk affect their frequency?
PPCs are unexpected postoperative pulmonary abnormalities causing clinically important disease or dysfunction requiring intervention. Notes report approximately 7% with normal preoperative lung function and rates as high as 70% with increased risk factors; respiratory failure is rare without preexisting cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disorders.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Why teach breathing exercises before surgery?
cards.a:
Why teach breathing exercises before surgery?
Patients can practice while comfortable and alert, before postoperative pain makes learning harder. Preoperative education includes deep breathing, coughing, early mobilization, and lung expansion techniques, preparing patients to participate in measures intended to reduce postoperative complications.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: How do the preoperative risk-factor notes explain smoking, cardiopulmonary findings, and ASA classification?
cards.a:
How do the preoperative risk-factor notes explain smoking, cardiopulmonary findings, and ASA classification?
Smoking promotes airway inflammation, secretions, and impaired mucociliary clearance. Low SpO₂, anemia, and CHF may signal impaired oxygen delivery or reduced reserve. ASA classification ≥2 indicates systemic disease, with higher classifications generally associated with greater perioperative risk.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Which age-related pulmonary changes increase postoperative respiratory risk?
cards.a:
Which age-related pulmonary changes increase postoperative respiratory risk?
Reduced chest wall compliance increases expansion effort; weaker respiratory muscles may reduce cough effectiveness and ventilatory reserve. Increased closing volume promotes earlier small-airway closure and atelectasis. Reduced elastic recoil contributes to air trapping, while increased V/Q mismatch can reduce PaO₂.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Why is chronological age insufficient for assessing surgical risk in older adults?
cards.a:
Why is chronological age insufficient for assessing surgical risk in older adults?
Overall health and functional status matter alongside age. Frailty, cognitive impairment, malnutrition, and functional dependence can impair recovery and participation in respiratory care. The notes define frailty as deterioration in physiologic reserves that prevents maintenance of homeostasis.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Why do obesity and suspected OSA require special postoperative respiratory attention?
cards.a:
Why do obesity and suspected OSA require special postoperative respiratory attention?
Obesity can reduce lung volumes and FRC while increasing work of breathing, and OSA may be undiagnosed. After surgery, anesthetics, opioids, and sedatives can worsen upper airway obstruction and hypoventilation, making recognition and monitoring particularly important.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Which symptoms and history make up STOP in STOP-BANG?
cards.a:
Which symptoms and history make up STOP in STOP-BANG?
STOP asks about loud snoring, frequent daytime tiredness or sleepiness, observed pauses in breathing during sleep, and high blood pressure or treatment for it. These items contribute to screening for OSA before anesthesia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Which body measurements and demographic items make up BANG in STOP-BANG?
cards.a:
Which body measurements and demographic items make up BANG in STOP-BANG?
BANG includes BMI > 35, age > 50 years, neck circumference more than 16 inches (> 40 cm) measured at the Adam's apple, and male gender. Age and gender are population-based risk indicators, not proof of OSA.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: How is STOP-BANG scored, and what does a positive result mean?
cards.a:
How is STOP-BANG scored, and what does a positive result mean?
Each positive response receives one point; higher scores indicate greater OSA likelihood. A score of 3 or greater is commonly considered a positive screen. Additional criteria may identify especially high risk, but STOP-BANG does not diagnose OSA.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: What postoperative plan may be appropriate for a patient who uses CPAP at home for OSA?
cards.a:
What postoperative plan may be appropriate for a patient who uses CPAP at home for OSA?
A patient with known OSA may need to resume home CPAP postoperatively when appropriate, together with monitoring for respiratory depression. This matters because anesthetics, opioids, and sedatives can worsen upper airway obstruction and hypoventilation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: How should surgical grade be used when estimating pulmonary risk?
cards.a:
How should surgical grade be used when estimating pulmonary risk?
Procedures are described as minor, intermediate, or major according to complexity and extent. Greater extent generally increases pulmonary risk, but location, type, and underlying health may matter more. Major surgery does not guarantee complications, and minor surgery does not eliminate risk.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: Why are spirometry and DLCO important before lung resection?
cards.a:
Why are spirometry and DLCO important before lung resection?
They assess whether the patient has enough pulmonary reserve to tolerate lung tissue removal. FEV₁ and DLCO help predict remaining postoperative function and identify patients needing additional evaluation; predicted postoperative values are calculated when appropriate.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::01 Risk & Preop
cards.q: What information should be gathered when assessing an older patient who smokes and has obesity before surgery?
cards.a:
What information should be gathered when assessing an older patient who smokes and has obesity before surgery?
Assess cardiopulmonary disease, OSA, diabetes, prior surgical complications, smoking exposure, respiratory symptoms, and functional status. Calculate BMI, screen with STOP-BANG, review SpO₂, and select tests when indicated. Determine the procedure's type, location, and anticipated duration.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraop
cards.q: What intraoperative ventilator settings do the revised notes recommend?
cards.a:
What intraoperative ventilator settings do the revised notes recommend?
Use VT 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight. Individualize low-to-moderate PEEP, often approximately 5 cm H₂O, to support recruitment without overdistention or hemodynamic compromise. Generally keep plateau pressure below 30 cm H₂O and use the lowest FiO₂ maintaining adequate oxygenation.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::02 Intraop
cards.q: Why use lung-protective ventilation during surgery even when the lungs were previously healthy?
cards.a:
Why use lung-protective ventilation during surgery even when the lungs were previously healthy?
It reduces the risk of ventilator-induced lung injury by limiting alveolar overdistention, or volutrauma, and repeated collapse and reopening, or atelectrauma. Previously healthy lungs can still develop atelectasis and injury during general anesthesia.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: How do pain control and early mobilization support postoperative breathing?
cards.a:
How do pain control and early mobilization support postoperative breathing?
Adequate pain control enables deep breathing and effective coughing. Early mobilization improves ventilation and reduces complications associated with prolonged bed rest. Lung expansion and airway clearance therapies are added when indicated to improve inflation and secretion removal.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: What safety teaching and respiratory monitoring are essential with PCA?
cards.a:
What safety teaching and respiratory monitoring are essential with PCA?
Only the patient should press the PCA button, never family or visitors. Programmed dose and lockout intervals limit medication delivery. Monitor sedation, respiratory rate, and oxygenation, because opioids can cause respiratory depression despite the pump's safety limits.

cards.d: Lesson 8::RCP 202 · 8b PostOp Respiratory Care::03 Atelectasis
cards.q: How does high inspired oxygen contribute to absorption atelectasis?
cards.a:
How does high inspired oxygen contribute to absorption atelectasis?
High FiO₂ washes out nitrogen, allowing oxygen to be absorbed rapidly from poorly ventilated alveoli. If gas absorption exceeds replacement, alveoli collapse.
